title: Binary search: halving your way to the answer
objectives: Explain why binary search needs a sorted array
Follow lo, hi and mid as the search narrows
Write binary search without off-by-one errors

blocks.markdown:
I am thinking of a number from 1 to 100. After each guess I say *higher* or *lower*. Guessing 1, 2, 3… could take 100 tries. Guessing **50** first throws away half the numbers at once, and halving every time, you never need more than **7** guesses.

Binary search is that strategy, applied to a sorted array.

blocks.question: How many comparisons does binary search need to find 9 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]?
blocks.explanation: It checks 7 (too small), then 11 (too big), then 9: three comparisons. Scanning from the left would take five.

blocks.title: One promise
blocks.text: If the target is in the array, it lies between lo and hi. Each comparison moves lo or hi past mid, so the range halves while the promise still holds.

blocks.title: binarySearch, executed

blocks.question: Why does the loop run while lo <= hi, not while lo < hi?
options: With lo < hi, a range of one element is never checked, so a target in the last position is missed
lo <= hi makes the loop faster
blocks.explanation: When lo equals hi, one candidate remains. lo <= hi still checks it; lo < hi would stop and report not found.

blocks.prompt: Arrange the lines into a working binary search, and fill in the blanks.
blocks.explanation: mid is the middle of the range. When the middle value is too small, the target can only be to its right, so lo moves to mid + 1.

blocks.question: How many steps does binary search take on n sorted items, at most?
blocks.explanation: Each comparison halves the range, so n items run out after about log₂ n halvings: 20 steps for a million items.

cards.front: What must be true of the input to binary search?
cards.back: It must be sorted (and indexable), or halving the range would throw the target away.

cards.front: Why is binary search O(log n)?
cards.back: Each comparison halves the range of candidates, so n items take about log₂ n comparisons.

cards.front: In binary search, what happens when values[mid] is smaller than the target?
cards.back: lo moves to mid + 1: the target can only be to the right of mid.
So a one-element range (lo == hi) is still checked.
